extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a mathematics textbook covering algebraic number theory (Artin reciprocity / representability of primes by binary quadratic forms) and introductory algebraic topology (quotient/product topologies, CW complexes, fundamental groups). Intended as definitions, theorems, examples, and exercises for students to learn and apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of two squares criterion (Z[i] factorization)
rubrics_metrics.description: An odd prime p can be expressed as p = x^2 + y^2 iff −1 is a quadratic residue modulo p (equivalently p ≡ 1 (mod 4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses factorization in Z[i]: if a^2 ≡ −1 (mod p) then N_{Q(i)/Q}(a + i) = a^2 + 1 is divisible by p, so p is not prime in Z[i]; factoring p = (x + yi)(x − yi) and taking gcd(p, a + i) extracts a nontrivial prime factor in Z[i], norms give N(x + yi) = p, so x+yi is prime. This argument generalizes to other forms x^2 + Dy^2 in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization to x^2 + 7y^2 (Theorem 63.7.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: An odd prime p > 7 can be expressed as p = x^2 + 7y^2 for integers x and y if and only if −7 is a quadratic residue modulo p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By quadratic reciprocity this reduces to whether (p mod 7) ∈ {1, 2, 4} in many cases; however, explicit behavior can be more complicated depending on arithmetic of the corresponding quadratic field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: failure when ring of integers not UFD (Example 63.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example p = 3 shows that even if some congruence a^2 ≡ c (mod p) holds, there need not exist integers x,y with p = x^2 + 5y^2 because the ring of integers of Q(√−5) is not a unique factorization domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: assuming 'gcd(p, element)' yields an element factor in rings that are not UFDs. Remedy: use ideal theory — lift (p) to ideals in the ring of integers and work with factorization of ideals instead of element factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: characterization via principal ideals (63.7.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prime p ∈ Q can be written as p = x^2 + 5y^2 iff (p) splits into p1 p2 when lifted to Q(√−5), where both p1 and p2 are principal ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reframes representability by the form x^2 + 5y^2 in terms of the ideal class group: whether the prime ideals lying above p are principal. Determining the class of p1 is the key arithmetic task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between principal ideal class and Artin symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: p1 is principal iff p ≡ (1) (mod 1) (i.e., the ideal class is trivial), and this condition can be detected via the Artin symbol in a suitable abelian extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Artin reciprocity in an abelian extension L/K (for example the Hilbert class field) to translate principality of ideals into splitting behavior (Artin symbol = id) in L: p1 principal ⇔ Artin symbol (L/K, p1) = id ⇔ p1 splits completely in L.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artin reciprocity: dependence of Artin symbol on p (mod f)
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the Artin symbol (L/K, p) depends only on the Frobenius class of p, which in particular depends only on p (mod f(L/K)) where f is the conductor/discriminant of L/K; if PK(f) = H(L/K,f) then this dependence yields a converse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplified statement: once you know p modulo the conductor f(L/K), you can compute the Artin symbol. If the congruence subgroup reaches the lower bound (PK(f) = H(L/K,f)), you also get the converse: knowing the Artin symbol determines p modulo f. Use Takagi existence theorem to relate subgroups of the ray class group to abelian extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ray class group correspondence and subgroup lattice (Example 63.7.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For K = Q and modulus m = 15∞, the ray class group C_K(m) is canonically isomorphic to (Z/15Z)× ∼= Z/2Z × Z/4Z, and each subgroup corresponds to an abelian extension via Artin reciprocity and Takagi existence theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: compute the ray class group and its subgroups to enumerate abelian extensions with given conductor; passage to sub-moduli induces quotient maps CK(15∞) ↠ CK(5∞) corresponding to field inclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction L = K(i) and its properties in Q(√−5) example
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K = Q(√−5) and L = K(i). Then L/K is abelian, the discriminant f(L/K) = 1, and H(L/K,f) = P_K(f); hence one can detect principality of primes of K by the Artin symbol in L/K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: for a prime ideal p ⊆ K, p is principal ⇔ Artin symbol (L/K, p) = id ⇔ p splits completely in L. Passing to L/Q, the relevant conductor is f(L/Q) = 20∞, so representability conditions reduce to congruence conditions modulo 20.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final arithmetic criterion for x^2 + 5y^2 (Theorem 63.7.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let p be a prime with p ∤ 20. Then p can be written as x^2 + 5y^2 iff (p mod 20) ∈ {1, 9}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is derived using the splitting/principality equivalences and Artin reciprocity for L = K(i) over Q, reducing the question to checking the Artin symbol which depends only on p mod 20.

rubrics_metrics.name: No universal modulus for some forms (Problem 63C)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no positive integer m such that whether a prime p ∤ m can be written as p = x^2 + 23y^2 depends only on p (mod m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guiding remark: certain binary quadratic form representability problems cannot be decided by a single congruence class modulo a fixed m; deeper class field phenomena intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of n-sphere and disk (Sn and Dn+1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard prototypical examples; exercise: the open ball Dn \, S^{n−1} is homeomorphic to R^n; S^0 consists of two points, D^1 is interval [−1,1].

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient topology definition (Definition 64.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a topological space X and an equivalence relation ∼, the quotient space X/∼ has points as equivalence classes [x], and U ⊆ X/∼ is open iff {x ∈ X : [x] ∈ U} is open in X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: D^n modulo boundary S^{n−1} yields S^n; identifying endpoints of [−1,1] yields S^1; identify segments of square to get cylinders/torus. Anti-pattern: when the subset A is not closed, X/A may fail to be Hausdorff (example: X = R, A = (0,1), then 0 and the collapsed point A/A cannot be separated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation X/A for collapsing a subset
rubrics_metrics.description: X/A denotes the quotient obtained by identifying all points of A ⊆ X to a single point while leaving others distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to succinctly express constructions like D^n / S^{n−1} = S^n. Be mindful of topological pathologies if A is not closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product topology (Definition 64.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given spaces X and Y, the product topology on X × Y has as a basis the sets U × V where U ⊆ X and V ⊆ Y are open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: one can use basis elements of X and Y to form a basis for X × Y. Ensure that familiar open sets (e.g., open disks in R^2) are open in product topology, even if not literally a product of two open intervals — the basis generates the correct topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjoint union and wedge sum (Definitions 64.4.1 and 64.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disjoint union X ⨿ Y has open sets whose intersections with each factor are open. Wedge sum X ∨ Y is (X ⨿ Y)/∼ where basepoints x0 ∈ X and y0 ∈ Y are identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: S^1 ∨ S^1 is the figure-eight. Exercise: disjoint union of two nonempty spaces is disconnected. Abuse of notation often omits explicit basepoints when understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: CW complex construction (Definition 64.5.4 and explanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A CW complex is built inductively: start with 0-skeleton X^0 (points), obtain X^1 by attaching 1-cells (D^1) via maps of S^0 into X^0, then obtain X^2 by attaching 2-cells (D^2) via maps of S^1 into X^1, and so on. Formally X^k = X^{k−1} ⨿ (⨿_α e_α^k) / ∼ where each k-cell boundary S^{k−1} is attached by an attaching map to X^{k−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology: k-skeleton X^k, k-cells e_α^k. Finite CW complexes use finitely many cells. Examples: S^n can be built with two cells (one 0-cell and one n-cell) or via hemisphere construction. Useful for constructing many standard spaces and computing invariants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attaching words for 2-cell attachments (torus and Klein bottle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The torus can be given as a CW complex with one 0-cell, two 1-cells a,b and one 2-cell attached via the word aba^{-1}b^{-1}. The Klein bottle uses attaching word abab^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting attaching words describes how the boundary circle of the 2-cell wraps around the 1-skeleton, encoding the fundamental group's relations; corner identifications in polygonal models produce these words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real projective space RP^n and constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: RP^n can be viewed as lines through the origin in R^{n+1}, as projective coordinates (x0:...:xn) mod scaling, or as R^n augmented with points at infinity forming RP^{n−1}. RP^n has a CW structure with one cell in each dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low-dimensional examples: RP^0 is a point, RP^1 ≅ S^1, RP^2 obtained by identifying antipodal points on S^2 (or by gluing edges of a polygon with appropriate orientation). Use coordinate descriptions to see points at infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex projective space CP^n
rubrics_metrics.description: CP^n is defined analogously to RP^n using complex coordinates (z0:...:zn) up to scaling; CP^n is like C^n augmented with CP^{n−1} at infinity and has a CW decomposition with one cell in each even dimension (D^{2k}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CP^0 is a point, CP^1 ≅ S^2 (the Riemann sphere). Useful in geometry and complex analysis; think of inversion and generalized circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concatenation of paths and homotopy associativity (Definition 65.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given paths γ1, γ2 : [0,1] → X with γ1(1) = γ2(0), define (γ1 * γ2)(t) = γ1(2t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1/2 and γ2(2t−1) for 1/2 ≤ t ≤ 1. This concatenation is not strictly associative on the nose but is associative up to path homotopy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with homotopy classes of paths (up to endpoint-preserving homotopy) to avoid dependence on parametrization; this gives a well-defined associative operation on homotopy classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of loops, nullhomotopy, and trivial loop
rubrics_metrics.description: A loop is a path γ with γ(0) = γ(1). The trivial 'do-nothing' loop 1 is the constant path at the basepoint. A loop γ is nulhomotopic if it is homotopic to 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize nulhomotopy as contracting the loop continuously to a point; spaces where every loop is nulhomotopic are simply connected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental group π1(X,x0) (Definition 65.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: π1(X,x0) is the set of homotopy classes of loops at x0, with group operation induced by concatenation *. The inverse of a loop γ is the reverse path γ(t)=γ(1−t), and the identity is the constant loop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify group axioms: associativity holds up to homotopy, identity acts as unit, inverses exist via reversed paths. Compute examples: π1(C) trivial; π1(C\{0}) ≅ Z (winding number); π1(S^1) ≅ Z; π1(S^1 ∨ S^1) is the free group on two generators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basepoint independence of π1 for path-connected spaces (Theorem 65.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is path-connected, then for any x1,x2 ∈ X, π1(X,x1) ≅ π1(X,x2). The isomorphism is given by conjugation with a path α from x1 to x2: [γ] ↦ [α * γ * α^−1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct mutual inverse homomorphisms using α and its reverse α^−1; these induce isomorphisms up to homotopy. Hence often write π1(X) when X is path-connected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality and invariance under homeomorphism (Lemma 65.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : (X,x0) → (Y,y0) is continuous and sends x0 to y0, then f♯ maps loops to loops and is homotopy invariant: if γ1 ≃ γ2 then f♯γ1 ≃ f♯γ2. In particular, homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic fundamental groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use composition to push forward homotopies. For a homeomorphism f with inverse g, f♯ and g♯ are inverse isomorphisms between π1(X) and π1(Y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher homotopy groups and basic facts (Section 65.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define πn(X) as homotopy classes of maps S^n → X. Important facts: πn(S^n) ≅ Z; πn(S^m) is trivial when n < m; for n ≥ 2 the groups πn(X) are abelian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret πn via cubes [0,1]^n with faces identified and define group operation by gluing on a face. Note that higher homotopy groups behave differently from π1 and are often harder to compute; a variety of exotic torsion phenomena occur (table provided).
